## Why 1-bit is hard

A binary weight is a sign, +1 or −1, and its magnitude comes from a scale shared by a group of weights. Two things make this difficult: sharing one magnitude discards information, and the scales themselves take storage.

### One magnitude for many weights

A 4-bit format gives each weight one of sixteen levels, so weights in a group keep different magnitudes under a shared scale. A binary group keeps only the signs.

Each arrow is one weight: direction is its sign, length is its relative magnitude.

The best shared scale is the groupâs mean magnitude [1] , and the error that remains is the variance of the magnitudes within the group:

\[ \begin{aligned} s_G^* &= \frac{1}{g}\sum_{i=1}^{g}|w_i| \\ \mathrm{MSE}_{G,\min} &= \frac{1}{g}\sum_{i=1}^{g}w_i^2 - (s_G^*)^2 \end{aligned} \]

For Gaussian weights with variance \(\sigma^2\), the magnitudes have mean \(\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\) and variance \(\sigma^2(1-2/\pi)\), and estimating that mean from \(g\) samples removes a \(1/g\) share of it:

\[ \frac{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{MSE}_{G,\min}]}{\sigma^2} = \left(1-\frac{1}{g}\right)\left(1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right) \]

This is 36.1% at group size 128 and 35.2% at 32, approaching 36.3% of the weight variance as groups grow. Quadrupling the number of scales buys less than one percentage point. The calculation is idealized and does not predict accuracy loss, but it shows how little a shared scale can recover.

### Scales cost storage

Smaller groups need more scales. A \(b_{\mathrm{scale}}\)-bit scale per \(g\) weights adds \(b_{\mathrm{scale}}/g\) bits to each weight:

\[ b_{\mathrm{eff}} = b_{\mathrm{weight}} + \frac{b_{\mathrm{scale}}}{g} \]

Lines use 16-bit scales. Dots use 8-bit block scales: NVFP4 [2] shares an E4M3 scale across 16 values; MXFP8, MXFP6, and MXFP4 [3] share an E8M0 scale across 32. NVFP4âs extra per-tensor scale is excluded.

With a 16-bit scale and groups of 32, the scale adds 0.5 bits per weight to every format. That is 33% of a 1-bit modelâs storage, against 6% of an 8-bit modelâs. Groups of 8 already cost 3 bits per weight at one bit, and a scale per weight costs 17, more than the 16-bit original.
